parameters.derivation:
JUDGE RULING: this follows neither synthesis exactly. It keeps their shared method and resolves three input disagreements in favour of documented values; details are under (c). The result widens A's range (6.84 to 20.60) at both ends, and B's range (6.8 to 20.9) at the low end.

(a) Method, shared by A and B and adopted. Only car motion goes into gamma; door, transfer, start and levelling times sit in load_time and unload_time. Flight time comes from the Peters jerk-limited formula (peters_rtt-6): t_f(d) = d/v + a/j + v/a, valid when d >= (a^2 v + v^2 j)/(j a). That condition is met at every corner: the largest threshold is 2.8 m, against d >= 5.48 m. The model charges gamma*|g-h| with no constant term. Under the protocol §11.2 mapping, loaded trips are 1<->2 and 1<->3 in equal shares, so gamma = [t_f(h) + t_f(2h)]/3, which keeps the total flight time of that mix exact.

(b) Inputs and their status.
- h, floor-to-floor height: 5.48 to 9.75 m, documented. The low end is the Goodman Interlink lift-access floors, 18 to 21 ft / 5.48 to 6.50 m (warehouse_floors-4); 5.5 m clear or effective heights (warehouse_floors-5, -6, -7, -8) confirm it. A clear height is a strict lower bound on floor-to-floor height. The high end is the 32 ft (9.75 m) floor-to-floor at Georgetown Crossroads Level 1 (warehouse_floors-1), applied to both gaps as an upper bound.
- v, rated speed: 0.5 to 1.0 m/s. The values are documented; the band is a case assumption. Sources: KONE TranSys DX 'Speed 0.5 or 1.0 m/s' (kone-9); KONE TranSys Asia 'up to 1.0 m/s' (kone-7); KONE HD MonoSpace 0.51/0.76 m/s (kone-1); Schindler 2600 rope 1.0 m/s at 2500 to 3500 kg (schindler_other-2); Barney Table 5.3, lift travel < 20 m -> < 1.00 m/s (peters_rtt-10); the case rise is 11 to 19.5 m.
- a, acceleration: 0.4 m/s2 at v < 1.0 m/s (Barney Table 5.3, peters_rtt-10). At 1.0 m/s it is 0.4 to 0.8 m/s2: Barney/Peters 0.4 to 0.7 (peters_rtt-7) and KONE 0.8 for 1 to 2 m/s lifts (kone-16, peters_rtt-14). These are documented passenger-lift values.
- j, jerk: 0.51 to 1.2 m/s3, documented for passenger lifts. The low end is Peters' measurement (peters_rtt-2); the high end is the KONE planning value (kone-16).

(c) Disagreements resolved.
(1) Jerk lower bound. A uses 1.0 and B uses 0.5. The only measured jerk in the evidence is 0.51, so 0.51 is used; dropping it would narrow the range.
(2) Acceleration at v = 0.5 m/s. B's 20.91 s corner pairs 0.5 m/s with a = 0.7, which no source documents; Barney gives 0.4 below 1.0 m/s. A's pairing is followed.
(3) Acceleration at 1.0 m/s. Both syntheses stopped at 0.7 and omitted KONE's documented 0.8 for 1 to 2 m/s lifts, so it is added.
(4) Low floor height. It is 5.48 m (Goodman, a lift-served multi-storey warehouse) rather than 5.5 m.

(d) Numbers.
- Fast corner (h 5.48, v 1.0, a 0.8, j 1.2): t_f(h) = 7.397 s, t_f(2h) = 12.877 s, gamma = 6.758 s.
- Slow corner (h 9.75, v 0.5, a 0.4, j 0.51): t_f(h) = 21.534 s, t_f(2h) = 41.034 s, gamma = 20.856 s.
- These are the minimum and maximum over all 16 documented-pairing corners.
- Midpoint = (6.758 + 20.856)/2 = 13.807 s. Record the range as (6.76, 20.86) and the midpoint as 13.81.

(e) Full references.

parameters.derivation:
JUDGE RULING: A and B agree on the structure and on each component range (8.30 to 19.15 s). I keep both and widen the high end for one documented item that both syntheses used only as a cross-check.

Structure: tau^L = D + t_in + t_sd.
- D is the door block at the origin: D = t_o + t_cd + t_c, with advanced opening t_a = 0. It follows the Peters/CIBSE performance time T = t_f(1) + t_sd + t_c + t_o - t_a (peters_rtt-1) and the Siikonen stop-time Eq. 20 (kone-19), with flight moved into gamma.
- t_in is one loaded AMR driving in.
- t_sd is the motor start delay of the loaded departure.

Components:
- Door block D, low 5.4 s. This is the KONE 1100 mm centre-opening row: t_o 1.4 + t_c 3.1 (same row) + t_ph 0.9 (kone-15, peters_rtt-14). Narrower-door rows (4.0 to 4.2 s) are excluded because AMR-capable doors are at least 1219 mm (schindler_other-18).
- Door block D, component-sum high 10.15 s: Peters measured t_o 4.31 + t_c 3.84 (peters_rtt-2) plus Sorsa's t_cd 2.0 (kone-17).
- Door block D, adopted high 11.0 s. This is the 'elevator door opening/closing delay' of 11 s from the AGV vendor handbook used for the Greenville hospital AGV elevators (warehouse_floors-13). It is the only door figure in the evidence from a dedicated AGV-elevator system. It is read as a lumped D, so t_cd is not added again. Excluding it would narrow the range below what the evidence supports.
- AMR drive-in t_in: 2.4 s (Smith 2018, robot loading time, peters_rtt-15) to 8.0 s (NAVER 'Fast' ideal boarding time at 0.7 m/s, warehouse_floors-15). NAVER's 16 s 'considerate' value is excluded: it depends on positioning among human passengers, which a dedicated freight lift does not have.
- Start delay t_sd: 0.5 s (CIBSE default quoted by Peters, peters_rtt-3) to 1.00 s (Peters measured, peters_rtt-2). KONE's 0.7 s (kone-16) and Sorsa's 0.6 s (kone-17) fall inside.

Numbers:
- Low = 5.4 + 2.4 + 0.5 = 8.30 s.
- High = 11.0 + 8.0 + 1.0 = 20.00 s.
- Midpoint = 14.15 s, exact.
- Without the 11 s reading, the range is (8.30, 19.15) with midpoint 13.725 s, as in A and B.

No double counting: door opening at the origin sits here and not in gamma. Door closing at the destination sits in tau^U, so a repositioning car arrives with doors closed and opens them here.

Full references:

There is no advanced door opening, and the start delay applies only to the loaded departure.

parameters.derivation:
JUDGE RULING: I follow Synthesis A in including the levelling delay and widen the door-block high end as for load_time.

B leaves out the levelling delay entirely. In this model it is charged nowhere else: gamma is ideal flight to level, and tau^L carries only the start delay. Leaving it out would drop a documented component (Peters Eq. 2; measured 0.61 s), so A's treatment is correct. B's resulting high of 18.15 s is therefore rejected.

Structure: tau^U = t_lev + D + t_out.
- t_lev is the levelling delay at the destination.
- D is the door block t_o + t_cd + t_c at the destination. The car is free once its doors have closed.
- t_out is one loaded AMR driving out.

Components:
- Levelling delay t_lev: 0 s (CIBSE Eq. 1 convention, peters_rtt-1) to 0.61 s (Peters measured, peters_rtt-2).
- Door block D: 5.4 s (KONE 1100 mm row plus t_ph, kone-15) to 11.0 s (AGV handbook lumped value, warehouse_floors-13). The documented component sum would give 10.15 s.
- Drive-out t_out: 2.4 s (Smith 2018, robot unloading time, peters_rtt-15) to 8.0 s. The 8.0 s is NAVER's boarding value applied by symmetry (warehouse_floors-15). No robot exit time above 2.4 s is documented.

Numbers:
- Low = 0 + 5.4 + 2.4 = 7.80 s.
- High = 0.61 + 11.0 + 8.0 = 19.61 s.
- Midpoint = 13.705 s. Record 13.705 so the midpoint is reproducible.
- Without the 11 s reading, the range is (7.80, 18.76) with midpoint 13.28 s, as in A.

No double counting: the start delay of the next departure is in that trip's tau^L, not here, and the door closing here is not repeated in the next reposition flight.

Full references: as for load_time (peters_rtt-1, peters_rtt-2, kone-15, kone-17, peters_rtt-15, warehouse_floors-13, warehouse_floors-15, same URLs and locations). Peters Eq. 2 with the levelling delay is on p. 60 of https://download.peters-research.com/library/Lift_Performance_Time.pdf. Access date: 2026-09-27.
assumptions: The door type, the passenger-to-freight door-time transfer and the lumped 11 s reading are the same as for load_time.
Drive-out upper bound = drive-in upper bound (8.0 s); only Smith's assumed 2.4 s is documented for a robot leaving a car.
The levelling-delay range rests on a single measured passenger lift (0.61 s); 0 s is the ideal CIBSE convention.
The car is free once its doors have closed. No parking dwell, and no 5 to 10% RTT controller losses (peters_rtt-8), are added.

parameters.derivation:
JUDGE RULING: I follow Synthesis A (1 to 20 s) and reject B (1 to 8 s), for two reasons.
(i) The task's definition of tau^P and tau^D explicitly includes 'lifting/lowering a rack'. The MiR Shelf Carrier lifts a shelf or cart, 27 mm (amr_service-8). Excluding it rests on choosing a case AMR class, and neither the protocol nor the evidence fixes that class, so the exclusion would narrow the range beyond the evidence.
(ii) B is internally inconsistent. It sets tau^P = tau^D, yet takes its 8 s high end from Kokhahi's raw pickup value alone. Under the symmetric model that source maps to its per-event mean, 5.5 s.

Mapping rule: where a source gives asymmetric pickup and drop-off times, the model value is their per-event mean, which keeps the per-order total 2*tau.

Documented per-event values:
- 1 s: Lamballais, Roy and De Koster 2017 (amr_service-1)
- 2.2 s: Xie et al. (amr_service-4)
- 2.7 s: Hai Robotics HaiPick A42T-E2 (amr_service-9)
- 3 s: Merschformann et al. (amr_service-2, amr_service-5) and the Lamballais thesis (amr_service-3)
- at least 4 s: Geek+ P-series minimum lift (amr_service-7)

- 5.5 s: Kokhahi and Kurz, (8 + 3)/2 (amr_service-13)

- Lindin: at least 2.4 s (amr_service-11)
- Interroll: 2.7 to 7.3 s (amr_service-10)

cross_checks: Arithmetic re-computed in Python for this ruling (no files written). gamma corners: 6.758 s (h 5.48, v 1.0, a 0.8, j 1.2) and 20.856 s (h 9.75, v 0.5, a 0.4, j 0.51). Synthesis A's corners reproduce at 6.841 and 20.600 s, so A's arithmetic is correct and only its inputs differ.

Regime check for the Peters formula. The largest threshold (a^2 v + v^2 j)/(j a) over the corners is about 2.8 m, below the smallest floor height of 5.48 m. So the rated-speed branch t_f = d/v + a/j + v/a is valid for every 1-floor and 2-floor flight.

Formula versus tabulated values. At 3.3 m, the ideal formula gives flight times 0.4 to 2.9 s below the Barney/Peters table values (7.0 s at 1.0 m/s; 10.0 s below 1.0 m/s). The tables include start and levelling delays, which this mapping charges in tau^L (0.5 to 1.0 s) and tau^U (0 to 0.61 s). gamma is therefore not inflated; if anything it is slightly optimistic.

Linearisation error. With gamma = [t_f(h) + t_f(2h)]/3, a 1-floor flight is under-charged by 0.64 s at the fast corner (8.6% of 7.40 s) and 0.68 s at the slow corner (3.1% of 21.53 s); a 2-floor flight is over-charged by the same amount. The total over the 1:1 loaded mix is exact (peters_rtt-4 non-linearity).

Convexity. gamma at the central inputs (h 7.615 m, v 0.75 m/s, a 0.55 m/s2, j 0.855 m/s3) is 11.49 s, below the range midpoint of 13.81 s, because gamma is convex in 1/v. The protocol rule (midpoint of the documented range) is applied as written and gives a somewhat slower elevator.

Speed-band sensitivity, not adopted. Admitting 1.6 m/s (Schindler 2600 rope up to 2000 kg; KONE TranSys EU) lowers gamma_low to 5.20 s. Admitting TKE EXPANSION traction at 0.3 m/s raises gamma_high to 33.5 s. The 0.5 to 1.0 m/s band is a case specification backed by Barney Table 5.3 (travel under 20 m -> under 1.00 m/s) and KONE TranSys DX standard speeds.

Double counting check. Door opening and closing appear once per stop, at the origin in tau^L and at the destination in tau^U. The photocell or closing delay appears once per stop, inside D; under the lumped 11 s reading it is not added again. Start delay appears only in tau^L, levelling delay only in tau^U, and neither is in gamma. Repositioning flights carry neither, which understates them by 0.5 to 1.6 s (a model limit).

Implied loaded trip, tau^L + n*gamma + tau^U (low / mid / high). One floor: 22.9 / 41.7 / 60.5 s. Two floors: 29.6 / 55.5 / 81.3 s. The mid two-floor trip (55.5 s) is consistent with the BCO goods-lift guidance of 60 s from loading bay to top floor (peters_rtt-17). The case lies between lumped simulation values (RAWSim-O 10 s per floor; hospital model 2.7 to 3.2 s per level) and measured robot rides in shared passenger lifts (86 to 374 s including waiting, warehouse_floors-17).

Performance-time plausibility, passenger reference at 3.3 m and 1.0 m/s. t_f(1) + t_sd + t_o + t_c = (5.1 to 6.6) + (0.5 to 1.0) + (4.5 to 8.15) = about 10 to 16 s. BS 5655-6 gives 8/10/12 s for excellent/average/poor, and CIBSE Table 3.8 says to consider replacement above 12 s. The low end sits at 'average' passenger practice and the high end is slower, as expected for wider freight doors.

Door-block plausibility. The documented component sum (t_o + t_c + t_cd) is 5.4 to 10.15 s. Author-derived freight-door strokes at the VA-required 0.3 m/s (schindler_other-17) give roughly 6 to 10 s per open-close pair. The AGV handbook gives 11 s (warehouse_floors-13). Using 11 s as the upper bound of D is consistent with both.

Drive-in plausibility. Author arithmetic: car depth 2.4 to 4.0 m (kone-8; Meitetsu 4.0 m) at the ASME-derived 0.365 to 0.5 m/s transfer limit (peters_rtt-16) gives 4.8 to 11 s. This overlaps the documented 2.4 to 8.0 s. The documented high of 8 s may be low for heavy AMRs in deep cars, and the 2.4 s low implies about 1 m/s entry speed.

Duty ratings, order of magnitude only (ratings are not cycle times). At midpoints a continuously busy car completes at most about 86 one-floor loaded trips per hour, within the Schindler rope rating of 180 rides/h but above the hydraulic 30/60 rides/h. This supports the traction assumption. At the low end (about 157 trips/h) the Otis Robusta rating of 90 starts/h would be exceeded.

Against the synthetic defaults (5, 2, 2, 5 s). gamma rises from 5 to 13.81 s (the default lies below the documented low of 6.76 s). load_time rises from 2 to 14.15 s and unload_time from 2 to 13.705 s; 2 s is roughly one door stroke, far below the documented lows of 8.3 and 7.8 s. service_time rises from 5 to 10.5 s, and the default of 5 s lies inside 1 to 20 s. The ratio (tau^L + tau^U)/gamma goes from 0.8 to about 2.0.

Differences from the syntheses. Midpoint gamma: A 13.72, B 13.85, judge 13.81. load_time: A and B 13.725, judge 14.15. unload_time: A 13.28, B 12.975, judge 13.705. service_time: A 10.5, B 4.5, judge 10.5. Every judge range contains both syntheses' ranges, except that B's gamma high of 20.91 s is excluded as resting on an undocumented acceleration pairing.

Status of warehouse_floors-15 (NAVER 8 s). Synthesis A's open issue reports a 403 and unverified values. The judge's input lists the item under verified evidence with section-level detail, and the failed list is empty. It is therefore treated as verified. The load/unload upper bound depends on it.

parameters.derivation:
The range is derived from documented inputs; no source gives it directly. The flight-time formula is Peters' jerk-limited formula (peters_rtt-6). At every corner of the input box the car reaches rated speed within one floor: it needs a*v/j + v^2/a = 0.83 to 2.01 m, and the smallest floor height is 5.5 m. So t_f(n floors) = n*h/v + K, with K = a/j + v/a. The model's gamma*|g-h| has no constant term, so gamma is chosen to keep total flight time right over an equal number of 1-floor and 2-floor flights: gamma = [t_f(1) + t_f(2)]/3 = h/v + (2/3)K.

Inputs:
- Floor-to-floor height h = 5.5 to 9.75 m. The 5.5 m is the documented clear-height floor (Meitetsu Komaki and KALOC 5.5 m, Prologis Japan >= 5.5 m, GB 51157 >= 5.5 m), used as a lower bound. The 9.75 m is the documented 32 ft floor-to-floor at Georgetown Crossroads Level 1.
- Rated speed v = 0.5 to 1.0 m/s. At the low end: KONE TranSys/TranSys DX 0.5 m/s standard; KONE HD MonoSpace 100 fpm = 0.51 m/s; Otis FOVF and Robusta 0.5; TKE traction 100 fpm. At the high end: KONE TranSys DX 'Speed 0.5 or 1.0 m/s'; KONE TranSys Asia and DX brochure 'up to 1.0 m/s'; Schindler 2600 rope 1.0 m/s for 1000 to 3500 kg; Otis and TKE traction 1.0 m/s.
- Acceleration a = 0.4 m/s2 below 1.0 m/s and 0.4 to 0.7 m/s2 at 1.0 m/s (Barney Table 5.3; Barney and dos Santos via Peters Table 1).
- Jerk j = 1.0 m/s3 (Sorsa; Khaleel et al.) to 1.2 m/s3 (KONE, Ruokokoski and Siikonen).

Low end (h 5.5, v 1.0, a 0.7, j 1.2): K = 0.583 + 1.429 = 2.012 s, so gamma = 5.50 + 1.34 = 6.84 s. This gives t_f(1) = 7.51 s and t_f(2) = 13.01 s.

High end (h 9.75, v 0.5, a 0.4, j 1.0): K = 0.40 + 1.25 = 1.65 s, so gamma = 19.50 + 1.10 = 20.60 s. This gives t_f(1) = 21.15 s and t_f(2) = 40.65 s.

These two values are the minimum and maximum over all 16 corner combinations. Midpoint = (6.84 + 20.60)/2 = 13.72 s (exact 13.7206). Start delay and levelling delay are not in gamma; they sit in load_time and unload_time. Door times are not in gamma either, because the Peters flight time runs from doors closed to car level.
assumptions: The drive is traction and the car is in the 1,600 to 4,000 kg class, large enough to carry two loaded AMRs. The AMR footprint and mass are not documented, so the car size is not derived from them. Hydraulic speeds (0.15 to 0.63 m/s) and 1.6 m/s (Schindler 2600 rope only up to 2000 kg; KONE TranSys DX 'higher speed on request') are therefore excluded from the band.

The lower bound on floor-to-floor height is set equal to a documented clear height (5.5 m). A real floor-to-floor height is larger by a structure depth that is not documented; Georgetown gives 1.22 m only at Level 1.
One floor height applies to every floor. Georgetown's upper levels have lower clear heights (24 ft and 16 ft) than Level 1 (28 ft).
Passenger-lift acceleration and jerk apply to freight lifts. No opened source documents freight-lift kinematics.
The motion profile is the ideal jerk-limited one, with no speed-reduction zone and no re-levelling.

The linearisation weights 1-floor and 2-floor flights equally. For loaded trips this follows from the protocol §11.2 mapping (storage floor 2 or 3 via hash mod 2). For empty repositioning legs it is assumed.
|g-h| = 1 means one floor-to-floor span. The US 3-floor cases (Georgetown, Red Hook) have freight elevators serving all floors.
parameters.protocol_fit: Partial fit. Rated speed comes straight from KONE and Schindler product data (plus Otis and TKE freight sheets, which agree on 0.5 to 1.0 m/s). The flight-time formula is Peters' (the protocol names the Peters round-trip-time decomposition). No manufacturer or Peters source gives a per-floor time for freight lifts, so the range is derived. Floor height had to come from warehouse case pages (DCI Engineers, Tilt-Up Concrete Association, Meitetsu, Kajima, Prologis Japan) and a Chinese national standard. Acceleration and jerk had to come from passenger-lift handbook tables (Barney via a scan, Peters 2000) and KONE-authored passenger-lift papers. The L2 addendum should call gamma 'derived from documented rated speeds, floor heights and lift kinematics', not 'documented'.

parameters.derivation:
Formula: tau^L = (t_o + t_c) + t_in + t_cd + t_sd.

This follows the Peters/CIBSE performance-time decomposition T = t_f(1) + t_sd + t_c + t_o - t_a (peters_rtt-1), with three changes: flight is removed (it is in gamma), the AMR drive-in t_in is added, and the closing delay t_cd is added. Advanced door opening t_a = 0 (the KONE and Khaleel assumption), so t_o is counted in full.

- Door cycle t_o + t_c, summed within one source row so rows are not mixed. Low: 4.5 s (KONE 1100 mm centre-opening, 1.4 + 3.1). High: 8.15 s (Peters measured, 4.31 + 3.84). Rows in between: Sorsa 4.7, Khaleel 5.0, Barney centre-opening 1100 mm 5.5, Barney side-opening 1100 mm 7.0.
- AMR drive-in t_in: 2.4 s (Smith 2018, robot loading time) to 8.0 s (NAVER 'Fast' ideal boarding time at 0.7 m/s).
- Closing delay t_cd (from the AMR clearing the photocell to the start of closing): 0.9 s (KONE t_ph) to 2.0 s (Sorsa t_cd).
- Start delay t_sd: 0.5 s (CIBSE default quoted by Peters 2012) to 1.0 s (Peters measured). KONE 0.7 s and Sorsa 0.6 s fall inside.

Low = 4.5 + 2.4 + 0.9 + 0.5 = 8.30 s. High = 8.15 + 8.0 + 2.0 + 1.0 = 19.15 s. Midpoint = 13.725 s; record it as 13.725 or 13.73.

No double counting: the door opening at the origin is in tau^L, not in the reposition flight. The door closing at the destination is in tau^U, so a car that repositions leaves with its doors already closed.
assumptions: Doors are power-operated horizontal centre-opening doors, as on KONE TranSys, Schindler 2600 C2/C4/C6 and Otis Robusta. US vertical bi-parting freight doors are not assumed; see open issues.

Door times documented for passenger doors up to 1100 mm wide (and one measured high-speed passenger lift) stand in for freight doors 1400 to 2100 mm wide. Wider and heavier doors are probably slower, so the low end is likely optimistic.
There is no advanced door opening (t_a = 0).

Drive-in time of a loaded warehouse AMR lies between a light service robot's lift loading time (2.4 s) and a 0.7 m/s delivery robot's ideal passenger-lift boarding time (8 s). No freight-lift AMR measurement exists.
One loading window serves the whole trip. In M2 a co-rider boards inside the same window at no extra cost; this is a property of the model, not of the evidence.
The elevator is integrated with the AMR fleet (call issued in advance, door closes on photocell or API signal), so the KONE default dwell of 5 s does not add to t_cd.
The start delay of the loaded departure belongs to tau^L, following the task's definition of load time.
parameters.protocol_fit: Weak to partial. The structure (door opening + door closing + start delay) is the Peters/CIBSE decomposition the protocol names. Door-time numbers come from KONE-authored symposium papers and Peters' measurement, but for passenger lifts. No KONE, Schindler, Otis or TKE freight product document states a door time: Schindler 2600 only says door speed is adjustable. The AMR drive-in term had to come from robot-lift literature: Smith 2018, a Lift and Escalator Symposium paper hosted by Peters Research, and NAVER CHI EA 2024. That source type is not named in §11.3 and must be listed as such in L2.

parameters.derivation:
Formula: tau^U = t_lev + (t_o + t_c) + t_out + t_cd.

- Levelling delay t_lev: 0 s (the CIBSE performance-time Eq. 1 has no levelling term) to 0.61 s (Peters 2012 measured value, used in his enhanced Eq. 2).
- Door cycle t_o + t_c: 4.5 s (KONE 1100 mm centre-opening row) to 8.15 s (Peters measured), as in load_time.
- AMR drive-out t_out: 2.4 s (Smith 2018 robot unloading time) to 8.0 s (NAVER boarding value, applied to exiting by symmetry).
- Closing delay after the AMR clears the door, before the car is free: 0.9 s (KONE t_ph) to 2.0 s (Sorsa t_cd).

Low = 0 + 4.5 + 2.4 + 0.9 = 7.80 s. High = 0.61 + 8.15 + 8.0 + 2.0 = 18.76 s. Midpoint = 13.28 s.

The door closing at the destination is counted here, so the next reposition flight (gamma) starts with doors closed. The next load starts with a fresh door opening, which matches a controller that closes doors after the dwell when the car is idle.
assumptions: The door type and the passenger-to-freight door-time transfer are the same as for load_time.
Drive-out takes as long as drive-in. Smith documents 2.4 s for both. NAVER documents boarding only, so the 8 s upper end for exiting is an assumption.
The levelling delay at the destination belongs to tau^U. Its range rests on a single measured value (0.61 s), with 0 standing for the ideal CIBSE convention.
The car counts as free for its next trip once the door has closed; no further dwell or parking delay is added.
In M2 all co-riders leave within one unloading window, so the second AMR's drive-out is not charged (a property of the model).
parameters.protocol_fit: Weak to partial, as for load_time. The door and levelling terms come from the Peters decomposition and Peters' measurements, and the KONE door times come from KONE-authored passenger-lift papers. No freight product data gives door times. Drive-out had to come from robot-lift literature. The only drive-out value actually documented is Smith's 2.4 s; the upper end is carried over from a boarding study.

parameters.derivation:
The model uses one value per service event (tau^P = tau^D). Where a source gives different pickup and drop-off times, the per-event mean is used, so the total service per order (2*tau) is preserved: MiR Shelf Carrier 250, (28 + 12)/2 = 20 s; Kokhahi and Kurz, (8 + 3)/2 = 5.5 s.

Documented per-event values:
- 1 s: Lamballais et al. 2017, EJOR (pod lift and set-down)
- 2.2 s: Xie et al.
- 2.7 s: Hai Robotics HaiPick A42T-E2 tote handling
- 3 s: Merschformann et al. 2018/2019; Lamballais thesis 3.0/3.0; RAWSim-O MAPF 3/3
- at least 4 s: Geek+ P-series 'minimum lifting time' (lift only)
- 5 s: Shan et al. 2024, tote retrieval
- 5.5 s: Kokhahi mean
- 20 s: MiR mean

Values derived from documented speeds:
- Lindin latent lifting AMR: 60 mm at under 25 mm/s gives at least 2.4 s.
- Interroll AMR top module: 800 mm at 0.11 to 0.30 m/s gives 2.7 to 7.3 s.

Range: low 1.0 s (the smallest documented value), high 20.0 s (the largest per-event value, MiR). Midpoint = 10.5 s.

The value excludes driving and any elevator time, so nothing overlaps with tau^L or tau^U.
assumptions: The case AMR type is left open: rack-lifting (Kiva/Geek+), tote-handling, conveyor top-module or cart-docking (MiR). The range spans all four, which is why it is wide.
Pickup and drop-off are symmetric in the model, so asymmetric sources enter as their per-event mean.
Fine positioning or docking under a cart is counted as service, not driving. It is included in the MiR figure and may be missing from the model-assumption values.
Values assumed in simulation and queueing papers (RMFS literature) are treated as documented values for a range, although they are not measurements.
parameters.protocol_fit: Poor. §11.3 names KONE, Schindler and Peters, and none of them covers AMR service at a storage or packing location; the researcher gap reports confirm this. The range had to come from AMR manufacturer data (Geek+, MiR, Hai Robotics, Lindin, Interroll/OMRON) and from peer-reviewed or preprint RMFS models. The L2 addendum must say that this parameter uses a different source type from the other three, stated before any case pool is generated.

cross_checks: Tabulated flight times versus the Peters formula. At the passenger reference (h = 3.3 m), the formula gives 5.3 to 6.2 s at 1.0 m/s (a 0.4 to 0.7, j 1.0 to 1.2) against 7.0 s in Peters 2000 Table 1. At 1.5 m/s it gives 4.9 to 5.4 s against 6.0 s. At 0.5 to 0.63 m/s (a 0.4) it gives 7.1 to 8.3 s against Barney's 10.0 s for speeds under 1.00 m/s, though Barney states no floor height. So the ideal formula runs 0.6 to 2.9 s below tabulated values, which evidently include start and levelling delays. In this mapping those delays sit in tau^L (0.5 to 1.0 s) and tau^U (0 to 0.61 s), recovering 0.5 to 1.6 s per loaded trip. gamma is therefore not inflated; if anything it is slightly low.

Performance-time check against BS 5655-6 and CIBSE Guide D. At h = 3.3 m and 1.0 m/s, the chosen components give T = t_f(1) + t_sd + t_c + t_o = (5.3 to 6.2) + (0.5 to 1.0) + (4.5 to 8.15) = 10.3 to 15.4 s. BS 5655-6 gives 8 / 10 / 12 s for excellent / average / poor, and CIBSE 2015 Table 3.8 says consider replacement above 12 s. The low end matches an 'average' passenger lift and the high end is worse than 'poor', which fits slower, wider freight doors. The door ranges are not faster than documented passenger practice.

Linearisation error. With gamma = [t_f(1) + t_f(2)]/3, one-floor flights are understated and two-floor flights overstated by K/3: 0.67 s at the low corner (8.9% of t_f(1) = 7.51 s) and 0.55 s at the high corner (2.6% of t_f(1) = 21.15 s). The total over an equal 1-floor/2-floor mix is exact. This is the non-linearity Peters warns about (peters_rtt-4).

Range midpoint versus central inputs. gamma at the central inputs (h 7.625 m, v 0.75 m/s, a 0.55, j 1.1) is 11.41 s, below the range midpoint of 13.72 s, because gamma is convex in 1/v. The protocol's midpoint rule therefore sets a somewhat slower elevator than the central specification.

Structure-depth variant. Georgetown Level 1 has a 32 ft floor-to-floor height and a 28 ft clear height, implying 4 ft (1.22 m) of structure. Adding that to the 5.5 m clear height gives h_low = 6.72 m. gamma_low would then be 8.06 s and the midpoint 14.33 s (+0.61 s). Using the clear height as the floor-to-floor lower bound widens the range downward, in line with lens A.

Implied trip times (tau^L + n*gamma + tau^U). A loaded one-floor trip takes 22.9 / 40.7 / 58.5 s (low / mid / high); a two-floor trip takes 29.8 / 54.4 / 79.1 s. For comparison: BCO 2015 goods-lift guidance says loading bay to top floor in 60 s (peters_rtt-17). Han et al. assume 40 to 100 s of elevator operation for hotel robots (warehouse_floors-19). Schulze et al. measured 86 to 374 s per complete ride for a button-pressing robot in shared passenger lifts, including call waiting (warehouse_floors-17), well above the model values, as expected. RAWSim-O assumes a lumped 10 s per floor per robot (warehouse_floors-18, amr_service-6), far below. A hospital AMR model assumes 2.7 to 3.2 s per level of running time only (amr_service-17), lower because of lower floors and faster lifts.

Door and dwell plausibility. Door cycle plus closing delay comes to 5.4 to 10.15 s, or up to 11.15 s with start delay. This is close to the 11 s elevator door delay in the Greenville hospital AGV handbook (warehouse_floors-13). Drive-in plus closing delay (3.3 to 10.0 s) fits within the 15 to 20 s door-hold timeout that vendors set for AGV boarding (warehouse_floors-20). Above about 4 s of drive-in it would exceed KONE's 5 s default dwell (kone-14), which is consistent with vendors extending the hold.

Drive-in derived bound. KONE TranSys car depth is 2400 to 3400 mm (kone-8). The ASME-derived transfer speed limit is 0.5 m/s, or 0.365 m/s for a 600 kg tug (peters_rtt-16). Crossing the full car depth at that limit, ignoring acceleration, takes 4.8 to 9.3 s. This overlaps the documented 2.4 to 8.0 s, but for heavy AMRs in deep cars the upper end may be about 1 s too low.

Vertical bi-parting doors. The VA manual says freight doors open and close at 0.3 m/s (schindler_other-17). Assuming each panel travels half of a 2.0 to 3.0 m opening height (kone-10), each stroke takes 3.3 to 5.0 s and a full cycle 6.7 to 10.0 s. That overlaps and exceeds the 8.15 s upper end, which confirms the centre-opening door assumption matters.

Duty rating and drive type. At the midpoint, a continuously busy car completes at most about 88 one-floor loaded trips per hour (3600/40.7), with extra starts from repositioning. That is within the Schindler 2600 rope rating of 180 rides/h (schindler_other-4) but above the hydraulic 30/60 rides/h. Two floors at 9.75 m (19.5 m rise) also exceed the Schindler hydraulic maximum travel of 18 m (schindler_other-3), while staying within the KONE HD MonoSpace 23 m (kone-2) and TranSys 23 to 40 m (kone-6, kone-9). Both points support the traction assumption. At the low end (22.9 s per trip, about 157 trips/h) the Otis Gen2 Robusta rating of 90 starts/h (schindler_other-10) would be exceeded. Duty ratings are equipment ratings, not cycle times, and are not used as tau values.

Service-time placement. The synthetic default of 5 s lies inside the 1 to 20 s range. RMFS model values cluster at 1 to 3 s, and manufacturer data run from 2.7 s (Hai) through at least 4 s (Geek+ lift only) to 20 s (MiR per-event mean).

Size of change from the synthetic defaults. gamma goes from 5 to 13.72 s, load from 2 to 13.73 s, unload from 2 to 13.28 s, and service from 5 to 10.5 s. The door and transfer time per trip, (tau^L + tau^U)/gamma, rises from 0.8 to about 2.0.
open_issues: No freight-door operating time exists in any opened KONE, Schindler, Otis or TKE document. The door-cycle range (4.5 to 8.15 s) comes from passenger doors of 1100 mm or less and one measured high-speed passenger lift. Freight doors of 1400 to 2100 mm, or vertical bi-parting doors, are probably slower, so the low end is likely optimistic. The author must state the door-type assumption (horizontal centre-opening, power-operated) in L2.

Measured drive-in or drive-out time for an AMR in a freight elevator: none exists. The range rests on a light service robot (Smith 2018, 2.4 s) and one ideal boarding design value (NAVER 8 s). The 8 s value is also used for exiting by symmetry.

Evidence conflict: item warehouse_floors-15 (Kim, Bak and Kim, CHI EA 2024, 8 s and 16 s) appears in the verified evidence, but a researcher gap report says the ACM PDF returned 403 and the values are unverified. This must be reconciled before L2 is signed. If the item is dropped, the transfer upper end would need the derived 4.8 to 9.3 s bound (car depth over the ASME speed limit, an author derivation), or the range would collapse to Smith's single value.

Freight-lift acceleration and jerk are undocumented; passenger-lift values are used (a 0.4 to 0.7 m/s2, j 1.0 to 1.2 m/s3). Barney Tables 5.3 and 5.6 were read from a scan on a university course page and must be checked against the book before citation. The CIBSE Guide D primary text was not seen.

No floor-to-floor height is documented for an Asian multi-storey warehouse with freight elevators, and no floor data exist for the Quicktron LH Nanchang case. The low end treats a 5.5 m clear height as a floor-to-floor lower bound. The high end is a single Level 1 value from one US building; the DCI page does not name Prologis, so the building identity rests on the tilt-up.org profile.

The speed band of 0.5 to 1.0 m/s is a choice: traction drive, car class 1,600 to 4,000 kg. Including hydraulic 0.4 m/s would raise gamma_high to about 25.3 s. Including 1.6 m/s (h 5.5 m, a 0.8, j 1.2) would lower gamma_low to about 5.2 s. The author must fix this choice in L2 before any case pool exists, not after seeing results.

Model limits of the linear gamma. Repositioning flights carry no start or levelling delay, so each is understated by 0.5 to 1.6 s. One-floor flights are understated and two-floor flights overstated by 0.55 to 0.67 s. The equal-mix weighting is an assumption for empty legs.

M2 interaction. The co-boarding window equals tau^L, so raising load_time from 2 s to about 13.7 s widens the window roughly 7 times and raises batching opportunities. The second co-rider's drive-in and drive-out are not charged. The one-at-a-time load_time and unload_time sensitivity runs therefore mix a delay effect with a batching-opportunity effect, and the case description should say so.

The service-time range is wide mainly because of one product. MiR cart docking is the only source above 8 s. Without it, the documented per-event values span 1 to 5.5 s (the derived Interroll bound reaches 7.3 s), giving a midpoint of about 3.3 to 4.2 s instead of 10.5 s. The author must decide before L2 whether the case AMR class is rack-lifting, tote-handling, conveyor or cart-docking, and record that choice as a researcher assumption.

Protocol wording. §11.3 names KONE and Schindler product data and the Peters decomposition. Only rated speed, and the decomposition structure and some door and delay times, come from those source families. Floor height (warehouse case pages, GB 51157), kinematics (Barney and KONE passenger-lift papers), AMR transfer (robot-lift papers) and service time (AMR vendors, RMFS papers) come from other source types. L2 should list every source with its type, describe gamma as derived, and keep the reporting wording 'parameters set within publicly documented ranges', never 'calibrated to a facility'.

Scale labelling. The case midpoints differ from the synthetic defaults by factors of 2.1 to 6.9. Case results (v0_6_case_*, config_id >= 100) must be labelled as the calibrated-case scale and never shown next to synthetic or publication-scale numbers without labels.

Recording precision. Suggested L2 values (s): case_speed_per_floor 13.72 (6.84, 20.60); case_load_time 13.725 (8.30, 19.15); case_unload_time 13.28 (7.80, 18.76); case_service_time 10.50 (1.00, 20.00). Record load_time as 13.725 or state the rounding rule, so the midpoint is exactly reproducible from the range.

If the elevator controller does not shorten the dwell for AMRs, the closing delay could be KONE's default 5 s dwell rather than 0.9 to 2.0 s. That would raise tau^L and tau^U by up to 3 s at the high end.

parameters.derivation:
The model charges gamma*|g-h|, and only motion time goes in gamma: door, transfer and start-delay times sit in load_time and unload_time. Flight time for distance d uses the Peters jerk-limited formula (peters_rtt-6). If d >= (a^2 v + v^2 j)/(j a), then t_f(d) = d/v + a/j + v/a. That condition holds for every d used here: the car reaches full speed within 1.0 to 3.3 m.

Inputs:
(i) Floor-to-floor height H is 5.5 to 9.75 m. The low end, 5.5 m, is the typical effective or clear height of multi-storey logistics floors (Meitetsu Komaki, KALOC, Prologis Japan Class-A, GB 51157 flat operation >= 5.5 m); a floor-to-floor height cannot be lower. The high end is the 32 ft (9.75 m) floor-to-floor height of Level 1 at Georgetown Crossroads, a 3-storey warehouse with 3 freight elevators.
(ii) Rated speed v is 0.5 to 1.0 m/s. This is the KONE and Schindler traction-freight band for the car class that can take two loaded AMRs: KONE HD MonoSpace 0.51/0.76 m/s; KONE MRL Freight DX 100-150 fpm; TranSys DX standard 0.5 or 1.0 m/s, higher only on request; Schindler 2600 roped 1.0 m/s at 2500-3500 kg and 0.8 m/s at 4000 kg; Schindler hydraulic up to 0.63 m/s falls inside. A real 3-floor freight group runs at 1.0 m/s (Kaufland). Barney Table 5.3 gives < 1.00 m/s for lift travel < 20 m, and the case rise 2H = 11 to 19.5 m is under 20 m.
(iii) Acceleration a is 0.4 to 0.7 m/s2: Barney/Peters give 0.4 for < 1.00 m/s and 0.4-0.7 for 1.00 m/s.
(iv) Jerk j is 0.5 to 1.2 m/s3: 0.51 measured by Peters, 1.2 in KONE planning.

Linearisation: under the §11.2 mapping, loaded trips are 2<->1 (one floor) and 3<->1 (two floors) in about equal shares. gamma = (t_f(H) + t_f(2H))/3 reproduces the total travel time of that mix.

Fast corner (H 5.5, v 1.0, a 0.7, j 1.2): t_f(H) = 7.51 s, t_f(2H) = 13.01 s, gamma = 6.84 s.
Slow corner (H 9.75, v 0.5, a 0.4, j 0.5): t_f(H) = 21.55 s, t_f(2H) = 41.05 s, gamma = 20.87 s.
The range is therefore 6.8 to 20.9 s, with midpoint 13.85 s. Across all 16 corners of the four input ranges, gamma spans 6.84 to 20.91 s.
assumptions: One uniform floor-to-floor height H for both inter-floor gaps (Georgetown shows the levels differ: 32 ft floor-to-floor at L1, 24 ft clear at L2).

The low H of 5.5 m is a clear or effective height used as a lower bound on floor-to-floor height, i.e. structural slab and beam depth taken as zero. No floor-to-floor height in metres is documented for an Asian multi-storey warehouse.

Two loaded AMRs need a traction freight car of roughly 2000 to 4000 kg. AMR mass and footprint are not in the evidence. Heavy hydraulic speeds (0.15 to 0.40 m/s) and 1.6 m/s (Schindler only up to 2000 kg; KONE on request) are excluded.

Freight-lift acceleration and jerk are undocumented, so passenger-lift handbook, measurement and KONE planning values are used. Pairing: slowest speed with the lowest acceleration (Barney's < 1.00 m/s row) and lowest jerk; fastest speed with the highest acceleration and jerk.
Ideal jerk-limited motion (Peters formula). Levelling delay, advance door opening (taken as 0) and start delay are excluded; start delay is charged in load_time.

The linear fit uses the case's loaded-trip mix (1:1 one-floor to two-floor). The same gamma is applied to empty repositioning moves, so per-trip error is about +/-0.7 s (a one-floor trip is under-charged, a two-floor trip over-charged).
The protocol midpoint rule is applied to the output range. Evaluating gamma at the midpoint inputs (H 7.625, v 0.75, a 0.55, j 0.85) gives 11.5 s instead.
parameters.protocol_fit: Partial. KONE and Schindler product data supply only the rated-speed range, and neither publishes flight time, acceleration or jerk for freight lifts. The Peters decomposition supplies the flight-time formula and the typical acceleration-by-speed table (from Barney). Floor heights had to come from warehouse case pages and a national design standard (GB 51157), and jerk from a KONE-authored passenger-lift paper and a Peters measurement. gamma is therefore the author's derivation from documented inputs, not a value read from a specification. The L2 addendum should say 'derived from documented rated speeds and warehouse floor heights with the Peters flight-time formula'.

parameters.derivation:
This follows the Peters/CIBSE performance-time decomposition T = t_f(1) + t_sd + t_c + t_o - t_a, plus the passenger-transfer and closing-delay terms of the RTT stop time (Siikonen Eq. 20). With advance opening t_a = 0 and flight kept in gamma:

tau^L = t_o + t_p,in + t_cd + t_c + t_sd.

Components:
(1) Door open plus close at the origin, t_o + t_c, paired within one door (rows not mixed): 4.5 s to 8.15 s. The low end is KONE's widest tabulated centre-opening door, 1100 mm (1.4 + 3.1). The high end is a measured installation from Peters (4.31 + 3.84). Barney's 1100 mm rows fall inside: centre 2.5 + 3.0 = 5.5 s, side 3.0 + 4.0 = 7.0 s.
(2) One loaded AMR drives in, t_p,in: 2.4 s to 8.0 s. The low end is Smith 2018's robot loading time in lift traffic simulation. The high end is NAVER's 'fast' ideal robot boarding time at 0.7 m/s.
(3) Photocell or closing delay after the last entry, t_cd: 0.9 s (KONE t_ph) to 2.0 s (Sorsa t_cd).
(4) Motor start delay, t_sd: 0.5 s (CIBSE default quoted by Peters) to 1.00 s (Peters measured). KONE's 0.7 s and Sorsa's 0.6 s fall inside.

Low = 4.5 + 2.4 + 0.9 + 0.5 = 8.3 s.
High = 8.15 + 8.0 + 2.0 + 1.0 = 19.15 s.
Midpoint = 13.725 s (13.7 s if rounded).
assumptions: Doors are closed when the load phase starts: the preceding unload_time ends with door closing, and a parked car is closed. No advance door opening (KONE, Sorsa and Khaleel all use 0 s).

Passenger-door times at widths up to 1100 mm stand in for freight doors. AMR-capable doors are at least 1219 mm (VA AGV minimum 48 in) and 1400 to 2100 mm on 2000 to 4000 kg goods cars. No OEM publishes freight door times.

Door hold is API-integrated: the door closes on the robot's boarded signal after one photocell or closing delay. Timeout settings (KONE 5 s default dwell, robot door-hold 15 to 20 s) are maxima, not durations, and are not added.
One AMR transfer per trip, as the task's definition requires. Under M2 co-riding (c = 2) the second AMR boards inside the same window at no extra time.
Robot transfer values from service robots in passenger lifts (Smith: assumed, light room-service robot; NAVER: ideal design value) stand in for a loaded warehouse AMR entering a freight car.
Start delay belongs to the departing loaded trip only. The start of an empty repositioning move is not charged.
parameters.protocol_fit: Partial. The structure is exactly the Peters round-trip-time and performance-time decomposition named in §11.3. No KONE or Schindler product document states door opening, closing, transfer or start-delay times: Schindler 2600 says only that door speed is adjustable. The numbers come from KONE-authored passenger-lift papers (Ruokokoski and Siikonen 2017; Sorsa 2019), a Peters measurement and the CIBSE default quoted by Peters, and Barney's handbook table read from a course-page scan. The AMR transfer term had to come from robot-in-lift studies (Smith 2018; Kim et al. CHI EA 2024).

parameters.derivation:
tau^U = t_o + t_p,out + t_cd + t_c at the destination. The car is free once its doors are closed. The next departure's start delay is charged in that trip's load_time, so it is not counted again here.

Components:
(1) Door open plus close, paired within one door: 4.5 s (KONE 1100 mm centre-opening, 1.4 + 3.1) to 8.15 s (Peters measured, 4.31 + 3.84).
(2) One loaded AMR drives out, t_p,out: 2.4 s (Smith 2018 robot unloading time) to 8.0 s. The high end assumes exit takes as long as NAVER's fast boarding time; no robot exit time above 2.4 s is documented.
(3) Closing delay after the last exit, t_cd: 0.9 s (KONE photocell delay) to 2.0 s (Sorsa door closing delay).

Low = 4.5 + 2.4 + 0.9 = 7.8 s.
High = 8.15 + 8.0 + 2.0 = 18.15 s.
Midpoint = 12.975 s (13.0 s if rounded).
assumptions: No advance door opening, so door opening starts after arrival and does not overlap gamma. Levelling delay is not included; Peters measured 0.61 s on one passenger lift.
The drive-out upper bound equals the drive-in upper bound (8.0 s). Only Smith's assumed 2.4 s is documented for a robot leaving a car.
Passenger-door times up to 1100 mm stand in for wider freight doors (same caveat as load_time).
Under M2 co-riding, both AMRs exit within one unload window (model abstraction).
The car is released when its doors are closed. Controller losses of 5 to 10% of RTT (Peters) are not added.
parameters.protocol_fit: Partial, for the same reasons as load_time. The Peters decomposition fixes the structure, but KONE and Schindler product data give no door or transfer times. Numbers come from KONE-authored passenger-lift papers, a Peters measurement and the Barney scan. The robot drive-out time comes from Smith (2018); its upper bound is an undocumented symmetry assumption.

parameters.derivation:
tau^P = tau^D is one handling operation at the source or destination (rack or tote lift or lower, or conveyor transfer), excluding driving. Documented single-operation times for these handling classes run from 1 s to 8 s:
- Rack lift/set-down in RMFS models: 1 s (Lamballais, Roy and De Koster 2017); 2.2 s (Xie et al.); 3 s (Merschformann et al. 2018/2019; Lamballais thesis 3.0 lift and 3.0 storage); 8 s pickup and 3 s release (Kokhahi and Kurz 2025).
- Manufacturer data fall inside: Geek+ P-series minimum lifting time 4 s; Hai Robotics tote handling 2.7 s; Lindin jacking at < 25 mm/s over 60 mm, at least about 2.4 s (derived).
- Interroll/OMRON conveyor top module at 0.11 to 0.30 m/s over 800 mm: about 2.7 to 7.3 s (derived).
- MTSR tote retrieval: 5 s (Shan et al.).

Range 1.0 to 8.0 s; midpoint 4.5 s. The synthetic default of 5 s lies inside.
assumptions: The case AMR is a rack-lifting, tote-handling or conveyor-top robot. MiR Shelf Carrier times (up to 28 s pickup, 12 s placing) are excluded because that module docks to and anchors a wheeled cart, which is a different mechanism from the model's definition.
Pickup and drop-off are equal (tau^P = tau^D), although sources give asymmetric pairs (8/3 s; 28/12 s).
Alignment or docking under the load is counted in service time only as far as each source's constant already includes it.
The 1 s low end is a queueing-model constant and is below Geek+'s documented minimum lifting time of 4 s. It is kept because it is a documented value for the same operation.
parameters.protocol_fit: None. AMR service time is outside every freight-elevator source named in §11.3 (KONE, Schindler, Peters), and no document of that kind addresses it. The range comes entirely from AMR manufacturer pages and data sheets and from peer-reviewed or preprint RMFS models. The L2 addendum must state this source substitution explicitly, with sources, before any case pool is generated.

cross_checks: The Peters formula (peters_rtt-6) matches the Barney/Peters single-floor flight table at 3.3 m and 2.5 m/s (formula 4.88 s against 4.8 s). At 1.0 m/s it gives 5.3 to 6.6 s against the tabulated 7.0 s. At 0.5 m/s it gives 8.65 s against Barney's 10.0 s for < 1.00 m/s, whose floor height is not stated. So the formula under-predicts low-speed flight by about 0.4 to 1.7 s per trip, and the gamma range may be optimistic by roughly 0.2 to 0.8 s per floor.

Implied single-floor flight at warehouse heights is 7.5 s (5.5 m at 1.0 m/s) to 21.6 s (9.75 m at 0.5 m/s). Documented passenger single-floor flights are 4.8 to 7.0 s at 3.3 m (Peters Table 1) and 10.0 s for low-speed lifts (Barney). The direction is as expected: floors 1.7 to 3 times taller and cars slower.

Kinematics hardly move gamma. Using KONE's passenger values (a 0.8 m/s2, j 1.2 m/s3) instead of 0.4 to 0.7 and 0.5 to 1.2 changes gamma by at most about 0.9 s at a given H and v (for example H 5.5 m, v 1.0 m/s: 6.78 s against 6.84 to 7.70 s). The range is driven by H/v.

gamma evaluated at the midpoint inputs is 11.5 s, against the midpoint of the range, 13.85 s. The gap comes from convexity in 1/v. Following the protocol rule (midpoint of the documented range) gives the larger value.

Door-related time at the origin (t_o + t_cd + t_c) is 5.4 to 10.15 s. The only dedicated AGV-elevator figure, a hospital AGV vendor handbook's 11 s 'door opening/closing delay' (warehouse_floors-13), lies just above the high end. This supports the upper part of the range for AGV or AMR freight elevators.

A derived freight-door check uses the VA requirement that freight doors open and close at 0.3 m/s (schindler_other-17). A 1.8 m centre-opening door gives about 3.0 s per stroke (6.0 s open plus close); a 2.44 m vertical bi-parting door about 4.1 s per stroke (8.1 s); a 1.5 m single-slide door about 5.0 s per stroke (10.0 s). The documented high of 8.15 s sits inside this author-derived 6 to 10 s band.

A derived robot-transfer check takes car depth 2.4 to 4.0 m (kone-8; Meitetsu car D 4000 mm) at 0.365 to 0.5 m/s (ASME dumbwaiter transfer limit cited as robot guidance, peters_rtt-16). That gives 4.8 to 11 s, overlapping the documented 2.4 to 8.0 s only from 4.8 to 8.0 s. The 2.4 s low end implies about 1 m/s entry speed, twice that guidance.

A two-floor loaded trip at midpoints takes 13.725 + 2 x 13.85 + 12.975 = 54.4 s. This is consistent with the BCO goods-lift guidance of loading bay to top served floor in 60 s (peters_rtt-17; office goods lifts, not warehouses).

A one-floor loaded cycle takes 22.9 s at the low ends and about 40.6 s at midpoints. For order of magnitude only (duty ratings are not cycle times): Schindler roped freight is rated 180 rides/h (20 s per ride), Otis Gen2 Robusta up to 90 starts/h (40 s), and Schindler hydraulic 30/60 rides/h (60 to 120 s). Only the traction ratings are compatible with sustained midpoint cycling, which is consistent with assuming traction lifts.

Lumped robot-elevator figures in the literature bracket the case. RAWSim-O assumes 10 s per floor for the whole robot transfer (lower than any documented component sum). A hospital AMR model uses 2.7 to 3.2 s per level of running time (passenger lifts and floors). A hotel robot model assumes 40 to 100 s per elevator operation. Measured real robot rides in shared passenger lifts took 86 to 374 s, including call waiting and button pressing. The case one-floor cycle of about 23 to 57 s (low to high ends) sits between the lumped simulation values and real shared-lift rides.

A measured 42.5 s door open-to-close when a human and then a robot board a passenger lift (Adachi and Kakio) far exceeds the case origin door-open interval of t_o + t_p + t_cd = 4.7 to 14.3 s. That figure reflects mixed human-robot boarding with announcements, which a dedicated warehouse freight lift does not have. It is not a like-for-like check.

Against the synthetic benchmark defaults, the default gamma of 5 s is below the documented low of 6.8 s, and load and unload at 2 s each are about 4 times below the documented lows of 8.3 and 7.8 s (2 s is about one door stroke). The default service time of 5 s lies inside the documented 1 to 8 s. With these values the case elevator is much slower than in the synthetic grid.
open_issues: Signing: the relayed request asks for a signature. Signing the L2 addendum, and decision D-K that governs case_included, is the author's own act and cannot be delegated. Nothing was signed or written here. These four ranges are a proposal for the author to check before they are copied into paper_draft/phase6_protocol_L2_addendum.md, and that must happen before any case pool is generated.

Protocol wording (§11.3) names KONE and Schindler product data and the Peters decomposition. Only the rated speeds (KONE, Schindler) and the decomposition, flight formula and passenger door times (Peters and KONE-authored papers) come from those source types. Floor heights, robot transfer times and all of service_time come from warehouse case pages, a Chinese design standard, robot-in-lift studies and AMR or RMFS sources. The L2 addendum should disclose this source substitution per parameter. Whether it counts as a deviation from the signed L1 text is the author's call.

Floor-to-floor height is the weakest input. The low end, 5.5 m, is a clear or effective height used as a lower bound, with structure depth taken as zero. The high end, 9.75 m, is one US building's ground level, and the second-level gap there is not published. No Asian multi-storey warehouse floor-to-floor height in metres was found, and the Quicktron LH Nanchang case gives no heights or elevator data.

Speed band choice: 0.5 to 1.0 m/s excludes Schindler hydraulic heavy-load speeds (0.15 to 0.40 m/s) and 1.6 m/s. Using the full Schindler 2600 span (0.15 to 1.6 m/s) would widen gamma to roughly 5 to 66 s. Hydraulic duty ratings (30/60 rides/h) would also cap throughput. The author should confirm 'traction, 2000 to 4000 kg car' as the case assumption.

Freight-lift acceleration, jerk and levelling delay are undocumented; passenger-lift values were used. The formula-versus-table comparison suggests low-speed flight may be understated by about 1 to 2 s per trip. A 0.61 s levelling delay (one measured passenger lift) was not added.

Linear gamma against non-linear flight (peters_rtt-4): the fit to the 1:1 case trip mix leaves about +/-0.7 s per-trip error, and empty repositioning moves (0 to 2 floors) are charged with the same gamma. This is a model-structure limitation that should be stated in the paper.

No OEM (KONE, Schindler, Otis, TKE) publishes freight door opening or closing times. The door range uses passenger doors up to 1100 mm, while AMR-capable freight doors are 1219 to 2100 mm or vertical bi-parting. The derived VA-speed band (6 to 10 s per open-close pair) and the AGV handbook's 11 s suggest the high end may be low, and the CIBSE Guide D door table was not accessible.

Robot drive-in and drive-out times for a loaded warehouse AMR entering a freight car are undocumented. The 2.4 s figure is an assumed value for a light room-service robot, and 8 s is an ideal design value for a passenger-lift robot. The drive-out upper bound is an assumption. Guidance-based arithmetic (0.365 to 0.5 m/s over a 2.4 to 4.0 m car) gives 4.8 to 11 s.

Co-riding: with c = 2, the M2 boarding window lets the second AMR board, and both exit, without extending load_time or unload_time. Physically a second sequential transfer adds one more t_p (2.4 to 8.0 s) at each end. The values above follow the task's one-AMR definition, and the author should decide whether that abstraction is acceptable for the case.

Door-hold and dwell: KONE's 5 s default dwell (adjustable 2 to 20 s) and vendor robot door-hold timeouts of 15 to 20 s were not added, on the assumption that doors close on the robot's boarded signal. A non-integrated elevator would add up to the dwell setting per stop.

service_time: the MiR shelf-carrier values (12 s placing, up to 28 s pickup) are excluded as a different mechanism; including them would widen the range to 1 to 28 s (midpoint 14.5 s). Sources show asymmetric pickup and drop-off pairs (8/3 s), whereas the model forces tau^P = tau^D. The 1 s low end is a queueing-model constant below Geek+'s 4 s minimum lift.

Secondary-source risk: Barney Tables 5.3 and 5.6 were read from a scanned course sheet, and the CIBSE values came via Peters 2012 and IMechE slides. Check them against the book or guide before citing in the addendum and paper.

Magnitude: the case phase times are much longer than the synthetic defaults (gamma 13.85 s against 5 s; load and unload about 13 s against 2 s). The case will be far more elevator-bound than the Phase 5 grid. This is a data-driven consequence and must not be tuned after results. The paper's wording stays 'parameters set within publicly documented ranges', with gamma described as derived.

verdict.reasoning:
I opened https://www.kone.us/Images/freight%20CSI%20spec_tcm25-125284.pdf on 2026-09-27. WebFetch saved the PDF (202.7 KB) and I extracted its text with pdftotext, writing only to /tmp and not inside F:/Paper 3.

What matches:
- **Header and footer:** 'SECTION 14 21 00 / ELECTRIC TRACTION ELEVATORS'. The footer on every page reads 'KONE Inc. ... Page N of 11 / HD Mono Freight Traction Elevator 09/22/2015 / Guide Specification / SF3136 14 21 00'.
- **The speed figures:** Section 1.11 SCHEDULE, item F 'Rated Capacity / Speed', lists:
  - '6000 pounds, 100/150 fpm (2722 kg, 0.51/0.76 m/sec.)'
  - '8000 pounds, 100/150 fpm (3629 kg, 0.51/0.76 m/sec.)'
  - '10000 pounds, 100/150 fpm (4536 kg, 0.51/0.76 m/sec.) (Available for class A loading only. See section 2.05 D.)'
- **Page:** these lines come just before the 'Page 4 of 11' footer, so they are on page 4 of 11.
- **Units:** the source states fpm first with m/sec in brackets, as the item says.
- **Section 1.05 PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENTS:** 'Car Speed ± 5% of contract speed under any loading condition or direction of travel' and 'Stopping Accuracy: ± 1/4 inch'. The ± sign shows as a replacement character in the extracted text.
- **Other schedule items:** B is 'Type: Gearless Electric Traction Machine – AC Drive', C is 'maximum 6' landings, and E is 'Travel: ... maximum of 75'-0" or 23 m'.
- **No timing data:** I searched for acceleration, flight time, floor-to-floor time and door timing and found none. Section 2.07 only says doors close 'after a predetermined time interval' and gives no number. The item's note that the spec has no acceleration, flight or floor-to-floor time is therefore correct.

One descriptor to tighten (the value and quote need no change): the document calls the product 'HD Mono Freight Traction Elevator'. It never says 'MonoSpace', and it does not label this product machine-room-less. The only mention of 'machine-room-less elevators' is in the installer-qualification clause. So the 'MonoSpace' and 'MRL' labels in the item's quantity field are not supported by this source. The paper should cite the product as 'KONE HD Mono freight traction elevator (gearless, AC drive)', or confirm MRL status from another KONE source.

Also note: 'Rated Capacity / Speed' is a schedule of options the specifier chooses from (100 or 150 fpm). It is not one fixed speed.

The paper also says its example criteria "do not represent requirements for any specific building type". Offices are mentioned only in the Introduction, as where up-peak traffic typically occurs. - **Start delay range:** The item's note gives "0.6 to 0.7 s", but this paper gives only 0.7 s. The 0.6 s must come from another source and should not be cited to this one.

evidence.notes: Open access (CC BY-NC-ND), DOI 10.1016/j.ejor.2024.05.016. The author was not KONE-affiliated in 2024 but led KONE traffic planning for decades. Eq. (20) is defined as 'where tc is door closing time, tsd is start delay, tf(1) is one-floor flight time, to is door opening time, and tcd is door clearance time'. verdict.corrected_value: Performance time (for the dispatching cost tau_ij) = door closing time at origin floor i + flight time between i and j + door opening time at destination floor j. Stop time, Eq. (20): t_s = t_c + t_sd + t_f(1) - t_pre + t_o + t_cd - t_v, where t_pre = door pre-opening time and t_v = d/v. t_s excludes passenger transfer times, which enter the round-trip time separately as 2*M*t_p (Eq. 19). Definitions only, no numbers.
verdict.corrected_quote: The performance time here consists of a door closing time at floor i, a flight time between floors i and j, and a door opening time at floor j.
verdict.reasoning:
I opened https://sal.aalto.fi/publications/pdf-files//papers/nor/psii24_public.pdf. It is the 12-page open-access PDF of M.-L. Siikonen, "Current and future trends in vertical transportation", European Journal of Operational Research 319 (2024) 361-372, DOI 10.1016/j.ejor.2024.05.016, CC BY-NC-ND. I extracted its text layer to a temp file outside the project folder.

(1) The performance-time definition is in Section 3.1, "Elevator dispatching problem" (journal p. 363). It sits in the paragraph on "Elevator cycle time cost tau_ij", which "includes passenger transfer times of call i and elevator performance time between call floors i and j". The quoted text is a verbatim substring of that sentence. The full sentence is given above; it goes on to "at floor j". The paper also says flight time is acceleration, travel at rated speed and deceleration (Eq. 2).

(2) Eq. (20) is in Section 5.1, "Calculation method" (journal p. 367). It reads t_s = t_c + t_sd + t_f(1) - t_pre + t_o + t_cd - t_v, which matches the item. The "where t_c is door closing time, t_sd is start delay, t_f(1) is one-floor flight time, t_o is door opening time, and t_cd is door clearance time" sentence is verbatim. t_pre and t_v are defined in the text around it, not in that "where" clause:
- t_v "is d/v, i.e. the travel time for distance d at rated speed".
- t_pre is "the preopening time of doors". The paper says "The elevator doors can start to open already in the deceleration phase", and that t_pre is subtracted to avoid double counting. The paper says "subtracted in Eq. (21)", which looks like a typo for Eq. (20).
The paper also states that t_s "includes elevator acceleration and deceleration times, door times, and other delays during a stop, but not the passenger transfer times (ISO 8100-32, 2020)". This matters for the tau^L and tau^U mapping: an AMR driving in and out corresponds to the separate transfer time t_p in Eq. (19), not to t_s.

(3) The note says the paper gives no numeric door or flight values. That is confirmed. The only numbers are waiting-time design criteria (30 s up-peak, 40 s lunch), car loads (1,600 and 2,000 kg), a historical 16.8 m/s speed and core-space figures.

Minor caveats on the notes, none of which affect the evidence claim:
- The paper never uses the term "ADO" or "advanced door opening". It describes the same idea as door "preopening" during deceleration.
- The paper lists the author only as CEO of MLS Lift Consulting Ltd (Helsinki) and Academic Visitor at Aalto University. It does not state a former KONE affiliation. It does cite KONE BTS simulations and many of her earlier KONE-era papers.
- The context throughout is passenger elevators in office and tall buildings under ISO 8100-32 planning, not freight lifts. So this item supports only the structure of the timing decomposition (definitions), not any parameter value for the freight case.

Peters' "Ideal lift kinematics" (IJEE, 1996) appears only as reference [8]. The formulae are due to Peters, but this paper cites them through [7], so the note should say "citing Al-Sharif et al. 2012 [7]; Peters 1996 is ref. [8]".

verdict.reasoning:
Opened https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.12318 (accessed 2026-09-27). WebFetch could not parse the text, so I read the saved PDF directly, page by page. The file is the PLOS ONE typeset version: Cheng L, Zhao N, Yuan M, Wu K (2023), "Stochastic scheduling of autonomous mobile robots at hospitals", PLoS ONE 18(10): e0292002, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0292002.

What the source says:
- **The quoted sentence (p. 14/24, Section 6.1 "Improved Solomon instances", modification (3)).** The quote is verbatim, with subscripts flattened. The same sentence continues: "μ (Vr) = 1.3s/m and μ (Vf) = 3.0s/level during the afternoon peak period, and μ (Vr) = 1.1s/m".
- **The non-peak value (p. 15/24).** It carries on: "and μ (Vf) = 2.7s/level during non-peak period. σ2 (Vr) and σ2 (Vf) are the same among the three periods. (4) The medical requests are distributed across floors 1 – 6, and the elevator is located at the center of each floor."
- **Table 2 (p. 15).** It gives the variance of elevator running time σ2(Vf) = 0.5 (s²/level²).
- **Definitions (p. 3, Section 3).** "the elevator running time per unit floor Vf (s/level)" is a random variable that "follow[s] a normal distribution with mean μ(Vf)". Table 1 (p. 6) defines Vf as "Elevator running time per unit floor".
- **Fig 1 (p. 4).** It plots μ(Vf) as a step function: 2.7, then 3.2 from 8:00 to 12:00, 2.7, 3.0 from 14:00 to 16:00, and 2.7.
- **Travel time (p. 4).** It is linear in the floor difference: T = d_ij·Vr + |f_ij|·Vf, with mean d_ij·μ(Vr) + |f_ij|·μ(Vf). This fits the linear gamma·|g−h| form used for speed_per_floor.

2. **The values are assumed.** They are set with "are assigned as follows", with no source given and no measurement behind them. The peak/off-peak differences reflect "hospital traffic", so μ(Vf) probably includes congestion and elevator availability as well as pure car flight time per floor. Section 4 (p. 5) says AMR travel time "is affected by environmental factors such as traffic, congestion, and elevator availability".
3. **There is no separate term for door or loading time.** Vf is the only per-floor elevator term, so it is not a clean equivalent of gamma.

The item's location "pp. 14-15" and its quote are accurate. I am not changing any field; the corrected fields above repeat the confirmed values and add the variance.

gaps: KONE freight-door operating times: no public KONE document found gives door opening or closing time (or door speed) for freight doors. This covers the vertical bi-parting doors on US HD MonoSpace/MRL Freight DX/MiniSpace Freight DX and the wide 2-, 4- and 6-panel KES 800 / AMD2 / AMD3 / AMD5 doors on TranSys. The only KONE door times found (kone-15, kone-17) are for 800 to 1100 mm passenger doors.

KONE flight times: no KONE product literature (TranSys, TranSys DX, HD MonoSpace, MonoGoods, freight web page, Architectural Planning Guide, MonoSpace 500 planning guide) publishes single-floor or floor-to-floor flight time, acceleration or jerk for freight elevators. Only rated speeds are published (0.5 to 1.6 m/s EU/Asia; 50 to 350 fpm US). Kinematic values (a 0.8 to 1.0 m/s2, j 1.0 to 1.2 m/s3, start delay 0.6 to 0.7 s) come only from KONE-authored passenger-lift papers.

Per-floor travel time gamma cannot be read directly from any KONE source. It would have to be derived from a warehouse floor height (not documented by KONE; KONE examples use 3.0 m and 4.0 m office floors) together with rated speed and kinematics, and that derivation would be the author's own, not a documented value.

AMR or robot boarding and exiting times, and robot door-hold settings: KONE's Service Robot API and Elevator Call API documentation (dev.kone.com) returned only a header without login, and the konecorp/kone-api-examples GitHub repo contains no timing values.
AMR pickup and drop-off service time (tau^P = tau^D) is outside KONE's scope; no KONE document addresses it.

Freight loading and unloading time as a whole (door stroke + vehicle drive-in/out + dwell) is not documented by KONE for pallet trucks, forklifts or AMRs. Only human passenger transfer times (1.0 to 1.7 s per person) and default door dwell (5 s, adjustable 2 to 20 s) were found.
KONE 'Elevator Planning: A Handbook for Architects' (kone.com, tcm17-75237) was opened and contains no door, flight or transfer times, only a checklist naming door type and speed.

KONE internal traffic-planning publications cited by Siikonen (Roschier and Virkkala, 'Planning of lift systems'; Roschier, 'Modern elevator traffic planning methods') are not publicly available. Siikonen (2000) 'On traffic planning methodology' was found only on a third-party mirror (silo.tips), gave no door or flight numbers there, and was not used.
The medicalexpo.com KONE TranSys and MonoSpace catalogue mirrors returned HTTP 403 and were not used. The KONE US 'High-Performance Door Systems' PDF link returned a 404 page.

No Schindler, Otis or TK Elevator freight document I opened states door opening or closing times in seconds. Schindler 2600 says only that door speed 'can also be adjusted'; Otis FOVF, Gen2/Gen3 Robusta and TKE EXPANSION give door types and sizes only. The only door speeds or times found are the VA design manual (freight doors 0.3 m/s), the TSSA closing-time table (horizontal passenger-size doors) and an Otis passenger door-operator claim (3.0 to 1.6 s).

No documented door opening or closing time for power-operated vertical bi-parting freight doors in seconds. The about 4 s per stroke in schindler_other-17 is my own arithmetic from 0.3 m/s and a 2.44 m opening, not a sourced value.

speed_per_floor (gamma): none of these OEM sources gives floor-to-floor (flight) time, acceleration or jerk for freight elevators. Only rated speeds (0.15 to 1.6 m/s) and max rise/stops are documented, so gamma cannot be taken directly from them; it needs floor height plus a kinematic assumption from another source (e.g. Peters, Barney, CIBSE Guide D).

load_time and unload_time as whole quantities (door open + vehicle transfer + door close, plus start delay or release) are not documented by any Schindler, Otis or TKE source. The time for a load-carrying vehicle (AMR or forklift) to drive into or out of a freight car is not documented anywhere I opened.
service_time (AMR pickup or drop-off service) is outside what elevator OEM documents cover; nothing found in this topic's sources.

Schindler 5300: no freight or goods data sheet found; it is a passenger or service product. The Schindler US freight web page (schindler.com/en/elevators/freight.html) lists no specifications, and no Schindler North American vertical bi-parting freight product data was found.

Otis North American freight elevators (vertical bi-parting doors, capacities in lb, speeds in fpm): no official Otis data sheet found. The MedicalExpo Otis catalogue returned HTTP 403, and the Scribd 'OTIS FreightElevators' copy was not opened because it is not a primary source.

Could not verify (HTTP 403): Vantage Elevation freight door and hydraulic specifications (search snippets claimed freight door closing speeds of about 0.8-2.0 ft/s), the Elevator World article on Peelle's high-speed door (HSD) system, and GAL's door kinetic-energy overview. These values are not reported.

Duty ratings (Schindler 180 rides/h rope and 30/60 hydraulic; Otis Gen2 Robusta up to 90 starts/h) are equipment ratings, not cycle times. Converting them to seconds per trip is arithmetic only and should not be used as tau values.

No opened source gives door opening or closing times for goods or freight lift doors wider than 1100 mm, such as the 1400-1600 mm doors of goods lifts or vertical bi-parting freight doors. Barney's Table 5.6 and the KONE tables stop at 1100 mm, and the CIBSE Guide D door-time table is paywalled and was not seen.

There is no measured drive-in or drive-out time for an AMR carrying a load into a lift car. The only lift-literature anchor is Smith (2018): an assumed 2.4 s per robot for a light room-service robot. Heavy tug robots were excluded from his traffic study.

The service time tau^P (AMR pickup or drop-off at the source and destination location) is not covered by any source in this topic, whether Peters, Barney, CIBSE, BS 5655-6 or the KONE papers. It must come from AMR or warehouse sources.

No single-floor flight time is tabulated for low-speed freight lifts (0.5-0.76 m/s) at warehouse floor heights. Barney 2003 Table 5.3 gives 10.0 s for under 1.00 m/s and 0.4 m/s^2 but states no floor height. Peters 2000 Table 1 stops at 1.00 m/s and assumes 3.3 m floors. gamma would therefore have to be computed with the Peters formula (peters_rtt-6), and the acceleration and jerk for freight lifts are not documented in the opened sources.

The CIBSE Guide D primary text (2010, 2015, 2020 or 2025) was not accessible: Table 3.4 on acceleration and jerk guidance, the door operating time table and the goods-lift section. The CIBSE values here come from the Peters 2012 figures and from lecture slides, which are secondary.

Barney's Elevator Traffic Handbook (2003, or the 2016 2nd edition with Al-Sharif) was not opened directly. Tables 5.3 and 5.6 were read from a scanned sheet on a university course page and need checking against the book before citation.

The Peters paper titled 'Understanding the benefits and limitations of the round trip time calculation' was not found under that title. The verified Peters RTT sources are 'Improvements to the Up Peak Round Trip Time Calculation' (2000) and 'Lift Performance Time' (2012). 'Lift traffic analysis: Formulae for the general case' (1990) was opened and contains no timing values.
Levelling delay is documented only as one measured value (0.61 s) and a small scatter plot (0 to about 4 s) in Peters 2012. There is no typical range stated in text.

No opened source documents the time a car stays unavailable after unloading (door closing plus any dwell before the next trip) for freight lifts specifically. The only values found are the KONE photocell delay of 0.9 s and the Sorsa door-closing delay of 2.0 s, both for passenger lifts.

Floor-to-floor (structural) heights: the only primary figure found is Georgetown Crossroads Level 1 = 32 ft. Georgetown L2-to-L3 floor-to-floor is not published. The Asian (Japan, Hong Kong, China) sources give only clear, effective or ceiling heights (5.5 m typical; Goodman Interlink 5.48-6.50 m; ATL 5 or 7 m; GB 51157 >= 5.5 m). No documented floor-to-floor height in metres was found for a multi-storey warehouse with freight elevators in Asia, so turning clear height into floor-to-floor needs an undocumented structure-depth assumption.

Freight elevator specifications at the named cases: no rated speed, capacity, car size or door type was found for Georgetown Crossroads' three freight elevators. The Quicktron LH Nanchang case gives no elevator count, capacity, speed or cycle time. Goodman Interlink, Meitetsu Komaki and KALOC give counts and capacities (5,000 kg; 3,500 kg; 4 units) but no speeds or door times.

Measured AMR/AGV boarding (drive-in) and exiting (drive-out) times for freight elevators in a warehouse: none found. The available figures come from service robots in passenger elevators (NAVER 8-16 s design values at 0.7 m/s; Adachi and Kakio 42.5 s door dwell with a passenger and robot), a hospital AGV handbook door delay (11 s, open/close split unclear) and a vendor door-timeout setting (15-20 s).

Elevator cycle time broken into phases (door open, transfer, door close, flight) for any AMR multi-floor warehouse case (Quicktron, Geek+, Hikrobot, ForwardX, Jiashun): not documented on any vendor page I opened. The vendor cases are qualitative.
AMR service time at source or destination (pickup/drop-off, rack lift or lower, conveyor transfer): not covered by any source in this topic.

Sources found but not opened (HTTP 403 or budget), so no values are reported from them: MDPI Mathematics 13(18):3031 (robot and lift schedules via SAT); MDPI Electronics 14(5):982 (multi-story path planning with elevator selection); ScienceDirect Procedia paper on elevator scheduling in a robotic automated parking structure (a search snippet mentioned 3.5 m floor height and 10 s door open/close, unverified); Daiwa House DPL Misato and CBRE Hidaka listings (freight elevator specs, unverified); Prologis property pages (403).
KONE Service Robot API: the public portal and the GitHub examples (konecorp/kone-api-examples) show no door-hold duration parameters, and the full API documentation needs a login.

The Hong Kong and Singapore searches were cut short: the web-search budget ran out (200 calls) before I could look for a Hong Kong or Singapore brochure stating floor-to-floor height and cargo lift speed. JTC Logistics Hub @ Gul lists ceiling height 11.2 m and 2.5 t goods lifts, but whether that applies to logistics floors is unclear, so it is not reported as an item.

No AMR vendor page or data sheet found states a set-down (lowering) or drop-off time. Geek+ gives only a 'Minimum Lifting Time 4 s'. The Quicktron M-series page (quicktron.com/products/m-series) and the Hikrobot Q7 pages (hikrobotics.com, absolutegauge.com) list a 60 mm lift height but no lift time. The Hikrobot Q7 data-sheet PDFs on DirectIndustry returned 403.
The Geek+ company brochure PDF is image-only; I did not read it, so any lift or transfer times it contains are unverified.

I could not open the full text of these peer-reviewed RMFS models, so their lift/lower times are unverified: Zou, Gong, Xu and Yuan 2017 (IJPR 55(20)); Zou, Xu, Gong and De Koster 2018 (EJOR 267(2); the HAL copy is behind a bot wall); Roy, Nigam, De Koster, Adan and Resing 2019 (TRE 122; the pure.eur.nl copy returned 403); Gharehgozli and Zaerpour 2020 (TRE 142; ScienceDirect returned 403). Boysen et al. papers were not reached.
The published journal versions of Merschformann et al. (ORP 2019) and Xie et al. (EJOR 2021) were not opened; their values are verified only in the arXiv preprints.

No documented drive-in or drive-out time for an AMR entering or leaving a freight-elevator car in a warehouse was found. The only numbers are a lumped 10 s per-floor robot transfer (simulation assumption), a 6 s passenger-elevator door dwell, and a 42.5 s mixed human-robot door-open time.

Kim, Bak and Kim (CHI EA 2024, 'Which Robot Do You Prefer When Boarding an Elevator: Fast vs. Considerate') reportedly uses robot boarding times of 8 s and 16 s at 0.7 m/s. The ACM PDF returned 403 and the abstract has no numbers, so this is unverified and not included.

The CHI 2026 paper 'Too Crowded for a Robot?' (doi 10.1145/3772318.3790593) reportedly gives about 15 s of robot boarding including entry and rotation. It is unverified (ACM access blocked) and not included.
No source states a roller or conveyor top-module transfer time in seconds. Only conveyor speeds (Interroll/OMRON, 0.11-0.30 m/s) were found, so any transfer time is a derivation.
The KONE Service Robot API portal and the KONE API example code gave no door-hold or robot boarding times. The Schindler robot-integration pages were not opened.

I did not open any case page for Quicktron with LH Nanchang or Prologis Georgetown (the multi-story AMR warehouses with freight elevators), so no site-specific AMR service or elevator-entry times are documented from them.

No source separates the AMR's service at the source location (tau^P) from the one at the destination (tau^D) with measured data. Only the model assumptions in items 3, 5 and 13 give separate pickup and drop-off values.
